title: Hollywood’s Worst Tendencies, in One Movie
text:
Prequels for long-running franchises are tough to pull off. Too many Easter eggs, and the whole project comes across as hollow fan service. Too different from the other installments, and the new entry risks not making sense. But The Hunger Games had a lot of potential to mine new stories from its past. Panem, the totalitarian nation behind the titular battles royal, had a turbulent history filled with cinematic potential, as well as complicated characters whose lives could be further explored. And besides, the original tetralogy, based on Suzanne Collins’s popular YA books, made more than $3 billion at the box office worldwide.

 In 2023, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes proved to be an uneven but inspired reentry . The film examined the teenage years of the villain Coriolanus Snow, and told the story of how the brutal Hunger Games became mass entertainment. The newest movie, Sunrise on the Reaping , follows a similar formula: It chronicles the coming-of-age of the series mainstay Haymitch Abernathy, as he’s forced to enter the Games and fight other youngsters to the death. Unfortunately, the film is a pale imitation of its predecessors. It looks like a Hunger Games movie. It sounds like a Hunger Games movie. But it misses the emotional and political stakes that had elevated the franchise above a once-crowded field of dystopian YA stories. If anything, it exemplifies Hollywood’s worst tendencies when revisiting beloved worlds.

 In the initial movies, Haymitch (played by Woody Harrelson) is a hard-drinking former Games winner who’s assigned to mentor Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), the strong-willed protagonist. He goes from dismissive and withdrawn to a pivotal player in the movement against the rulers of Panem. A prequel could not only fill in the blanks about his character arc but also scrutinize how revolutions tend to begin in fits and starts—and how maintaining passion for resistance can be much harder than it already seems.

 [ Read: Cinema’s newest, grimmest trend ] 

 Unfortunately, Sunrise isn’t up to the task. Directed by Francis Lawrence, the franchise’s steward since the standout Catching Fire , the film covers an unwieldy amount of narrative ground. The movie begins with 16-year-old Haymitch (Joseph Zada) participating in the Second Quarter Quell, a special edition of the Games that doubles the number of competitors, known as “tributes”; its epilogue catches up with Haymitch decades into the future, at the end of the Hunger Games series. In between, Haymitch meets a parade of one-note fellow challengers, delivers interminable monologues about Panem’s broken system, and joins a rushed conspiracy to dismantle the Games from within. The increase in competitors and plot points, however, yields only threadbare momentum and perfunctory thrills. What could have been a potent study of the consequences of believing in an abstract future becomes a hackneyed tale of unavoidable tragedy.

 Part of the issue comes from how indebted the prequel is to the other installments. Sunrise uses familiar setups: The reaping, the lottery through which tributes are chosen, is staged the same way as it was in The Hunger Games , all greige outfits and over-the-top theatrics from the tributes’ escort, Drusilla (an eye-searingly yassified but delightfully hammy Glenn Close). Haymitch visits his love interest in idyllic fields, just as Katniss (and Snow, in Ballad ) did. Younger versions of characters from the original tetralogy make brief appearances, each spouting dialogue nodding to things their older selves say in those films. These cues may be intended to emphasize how history repeats itself, but they drain Sunrise of fresh nuance. The movie seems more preoccupied with this nostalgia bait than it is with Haymitch, never interrogating why he is vulnerable to being recruited into a cause he barely understands.

 Then again, one of the biggest draws of The Hunger Games has always been the Games themselves. The franchise has tried to make clear how violent and wrong they are, yet on this front, Sunrise also falls short. The spectacle consists mostly of choppy action sequences involving characters whom audiences never get to invest in. Some of the deaths are appallingly inventive—one boy is eaten alive by carnivorous squirrels—but they’re hamstrung by the CGI sludge that makes up the bulk of the arena’s threats. The lackluster visuals may help dilute the horror of watching children get hurt, but they also make for uncharacteristically bland set pieces.

 The result is a long shrug of a film that, on the whole, seems thoroughly underdeveloped. Most of the new, more than capable actors, such as Lili Taylor, Maya Hawke, McKenna Grace, and Ben Wang, go wasted in thankless parts. (Jesse Plemons emerges unscathed, standing out from the ensemble the same way his role’s predecessor, Philip Seymour Hoffman, did with an understated performance.) The best entries in the franchise have balanced bloodshed with heady ideas about class, complicity, and youthful righteousness—and Sunrise , with its many homages to those films, clearly understands how much it owes to its forebears. It just never finds a perspective of its own.
